title: "Is that so?"
hook: the story of Hakuin, falsely blamed for a baby, who says "is that so?" and cares for the child

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basho's old pond: a frog jumps in, the sound of water, nothing added. Your line: the sound of water. Did a tap or the rain get to be the whole poem? Day one thousand five.

Angry parents are pounding on a temple door. Their unmarried daughter is pregnant, and when they pressed her to name the father, she named the respected Zen master who lives in the village temple. The whole neighborhood has heard. The parents shout their accusation in his face. The master listens, and says three words: Is that so? That's all. No denial. No speech. The story is told about Hakuin, a Japanese Zen teacher, and today we follow it to the end.
screen: `ANGRY PARENTS AT THE DOOR.` → `THEY BLAME THE MASTER.` → `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: First, a word about where this comes from. It's a story people tell about Hakuin, and nobody can say whether it happened as told. But it has traveled because it shows something clearly. Here's how it goes on. When the baby is born, the family brings the infant to Hakuin and leaves the child with him. You did this, so you raise it. Hakuin's reputation is gone. People stop coming to hear him. He says, Is that so? And he takes the baby. He begs milk from neighbors and whatever else the child needs, and he looks after the little one with care. Time passes. Then the young mother can't bear it anymore. She tells her parents the truth: the real father is a young man who works in the fish market. The parents rush back to the temple, ashamed. They apologize, over and over, and ask for the child back. Hakuin hands the baby over, and says: Is that so? Notice what the three words are doing. The first time, they aren't agreement, and they aren't a lie. They're a refusal to fight about his own name while a baby needs looking after. The second time, they aren't triumph. No I told you so. Praise and blame come and go, and he treats them the same way, like weather. And through all of it, the one thing that doesn't change is the care. The story isn't asking anyone to accept every false charge in silence. Some readers hear it as a story about ego: how little Hakuin needed to be seen as right. Others hear it about attention: whatever people were saying, he kept his eyes on the child.
screen: `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `HE TAKES THE BABY, AND CARES.` · `THE TRUTH COMES OUT.` · `PRAISE AND BLAME, LIKE WEATHER.` · then, large: `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: answer one accusation calmly, here, in rehearsal. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a small criticism you've heard lately, fair or unfair. Not the worst one. A small one. Notice what rises in the body: heat, a tight jaw, a speech getting ready. Let all that be there. Then, silently, try Hakuin's words: is that so? Feel the space they open, before any reply. You can still answer later, and correct the record if you need to. For now, just breathe in the space. The bell holds the time.
Hakuin. The Zen teacher the story gives three words, is that so, for blame and praise alike, while he keeps caring for the child. Today's word.
Your line: blame and praise, like weather. Today, when someone tells you what you are, good or bad, try saying to yourself, is that so, before you answer. Day one thousand five.

howItsDone: Zen teachers and Buddhist writers retell the Is that so? story as a teaching on equanimity, and Buddhist teachers present praise and blame alike as passing conditions, an old theme in the Buddha's teaching.

fork.setup: the parents come back, ashamed, and beg for the child. you're Hakuin, with your name restored. what do you say?
fork.reveal: he hands the baby back with the same three words he used for the blame.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite way to dodge an argument.
what it means: meeting blame and praise the same way, while care for the child never changes.
what a scholar hears: a story attached to Hakuin's name that echoes the old teaching on praise and blame.

notes: The story is best known in English from a modern collection (Senzaki and Reps) that is under copyright; retold in fresh words and framed as 'a story people tell', not from Hakuin's writings. Confirm framing.
Detail that the father worked in the fish market follows the common telling; confirm or drop.
The Dhammapada verse on praise and blame is cited as background, paraphrased, not quoted in the voice; confirm it is the right verse (81 in Müller's numbering).
howItsDone calls praise and blame 'one of the old themes of the Buddha's teaching' (the eight worldly conditions); confirm.
The practice is a rehearsal on a small criticism, with an explicit note that correcting the record is still allowed; check tone.
No original-language form: the Japanese wording of the reply in the story is not attested in a source I can cite.
